Chapter 1 Introduction 1.1 Integrated Gene Set Query 1.2 Launch project saved on server 1.3 ShinyOne

Chapter 1 Introduction The Quickomics tool can be accessed via the link https://quickomics.bxgenomics.com. Implemented through R Shiny, it helps with visualizing statistical analysis results for RNAseq and Proteomics datasets. This supplemental tutorial provides a detailed guide on using the different functionalities and customizing the tools to best fit individual analysis and plotting needs, using published RNAseq dataset and proteomics dataset as examples (Gyoneva et al., 2019; Connor-Robson et al., 2019). The interface contains multiple tabs, corresponding to different functional modules, that can be accessed on top panel of the webpage. Users have the option to upload their own dataset or choose from existing demo datasets for visualization. 1.1 Integrated Gene Set Query To supply genes in pre-defined gene sets to plotting functions in Quickomics, we developed xGenesets API for Quickomics to query and retrieve a list of genes/proteins when it is needed. The lists can be defined based on pathways, and gene sets from various sources, including KEGG Pathways (Kanehisa and Goto, 2000), WikiPathways (Martens et al., 2020), Small Molecule Pathway Database (Frolkis et al., 2010), Reactome (Jassal et al., 2020), Gene Ontology (The Gene Ontology Consortium, 2019), Molecular Signatures (Subramanian et al., 2005; Liberzon et al., 2015), and LIPID MAPS Proteome Database (Cotter et al., 2006). xGenesets database currently has 175,537 gene sets stored in MySQL tables, covering human (115,497 records), mouse (30,554 records) and rat (29,486 records) gene sets. xGenesets features personalized settings, dynamic drop-down list upon typing for quick gene set selection, full gene set database browsing, and a list of genes from any gene sets. Throughout Quickomics, users interact with this convenient tool in appropriate interface when a gene set is needed by checking “Geneset” option and then clicking on “Select Geneset” to pick a set from a table of available gene sets in a popup window as shown in the following screenshot. For developers of web-based applications (general user can skip this paragraph), xGenesets can be easily embedded in any modern websites and online applications, e.g., R Shiny web apps, by leveraging jQuery, DataTables, and bootstrap (either v3 or v4) JavaScript libraries. xGenesets API is freely available for all usages. Examples of using xGenesets API and guidance on setting up the API in your own applications can be found at https://bxaf.net/genesets. 1.2 Launch project saved on server In this updated version 2.0 of Quickomics, we added this new function to launch projects saved on the server directly using URL. To view your own datasets, you can upload RData files using browser, but a better way is to put the RData files on your server where you host QuickOmics and access them directly using a URL. We suggest the following: 1. Prepare three files for each project, projectID.RData and projectID_network.RData file, as well as a projectID.csv file. The csv file should have four columns: Name,ShortName,ProjectID,Species Two optional columns for the csv file include: ExpressionUnit (you can enter something like log2(TPM+0.1)), and Path (optional path for raw or analyzed data, e.g. Z:/share/GSE158470/). 2. Put the three files you prepared in a special folder, and use URL to access them. The simplest way is to put the three files in the unlisted/ folder under Quickomics folder. Then use a URL like https://quickomics.bxgenomics.com/?unlisted=ProjectID (replace quickomics.bxgenomics.com with your own instance URL). You can also create a config.csv file under Quickomics folder, for example: category,value server_dir, /hpc/data/server_files test_dir,/hpc/data/test_fiels Just make sure the two folders in server_dir and test_dir can be read by the Shiny App. Then you can copy the three files prepared in step 1) into the server_dir, and use URL like https://quickomics.bxgenomics.com/?serverfile=ProjectID Or you can copy the three files prepared in step 1) into the test_dir, and use URL like https://quickomics.bxgenomics.com/?testfile=ProjectID Using config.csv is preferred as the data are separated from the QuickOmics Shiny App folder. 1.3 ShinyOne In Quickomics v2.0, we also introduce ShinyOne, a web-based table listing existing projects loaded into Quickomics. We have pre-loaded several demo data to Quickomics, and the ShinyOne demo site is: http://demo.bxgenomics.com:8185/

Chapter 2 Dataset Module 2.1 Upload Files 2.2 Prepare R Data Files by Computational Biologists 2.3 Sample Table 2.4 Project Overview 2.5 Result Table 2.6 Data Table 2.7 Protein Gene Names 2.8 Help

Chapter 2 Dataset Module This first module is for selecting dataset. Users can either select from pre-loaded example datasets or upload their own dataset in a pre-defined format as detailed in section 2.1 and in our GitHub page (https://github.com/interactivereport/Quickomics). We have pre-loaded four datasets from published studies that users can use for demonstrative purposes. These includes two RNAseq datasets from Gyoneva et al., 2019 and Connor-Robson et al., 2019; and two proteomics datasets from Connor-Robson et al., 2019. Users can walk through multiple sub-tabs to visualize, select and download figures or data. 2.1 Upload Files The “Upload Files” tab allows users to upload their own data to Quickomics as csv (Comma Separated Values) files. Two kinds of uploads are supported: a complete data set, with a sample metadata file, a normalized expression data file and a statistical comparison results file, or a comparison data file only. Example csv files for RNA-Seq (200 genes from the mouse microglia dataset) and proteomics (200 proteins from the AD/PD dataset) can be downloaded from the links at the top of the tab. To upload, enter a project name, select the species (human, mouse or rat) and choose the files. Detailed formatting guidance is outlined below, Sample Metadata File: It should have “sampleid” and “group” columns, with additional columns optional. Sample identifiers must match those used in the expression data file. This file is not needed for a comparison-only upload. Expression Data File: It should be a matrix of expression values with genes/proteins as rows, and samples as columns. The unique IDs for genes/proteins are in the first column. We recommend using log of normalized expression values, e.g. log2(TPM+1) for RNAseq data or normalized intensity or ratio for proteomics data. The file can be compressed as .gz or .zip. This file is not needed for a comparison-only upload. Comparison Data File: It should have five columns, “UniqueID”, “test”, “Adj.P.Value”, “P.Value” and “logFC”. The comparison names are listed in “test” column. Please note that wrongly named column headers will cause issues. The file can be a csv or txt file, and can be compressed as .gz or .zip. Gene/Protein Name File: By default, Quickomics creates this file from the unique IDs in the data files, so most users don’t need to prepare it; select the type of the unique IDs, which can be Ensembl Gene ID, Gene Symbol, NCBI GeneID, UniProtKB Protein ID or UniProt Protein Name. To upload your own file instead, uncheck “Create Gene/Protein Name File automatically”. It must have four columns: “id” (sequential numbers like 1,2,3 … …), “UniqueID” (matching IDs used in the expression and comparison data file), “Gene.Name” (official gene symbols), “Protein.ID” (UniProt protein IDs, or keep it empty for RNA-Seq data). Additional columns (e.g. gene biotype) are optional. Then click “Submit Data”. After the data files are processed, Quickomics will automatically load all required data for exploration immediately and show a direct URL for the dataset, so that users can come back to it in the future. Behind the scene, gene IDs (Ensembl gene, NCBI gene ID, etc.) are converted into gene symbols by querying the Ensembl BioMart service. If BioMart cannot be reached, a built-in Ensembl annotation table is used instead, or g:Profiler as a last resort, and a note is shown when a backup is used. For protein IDs, we generated a custom lookup table using information downloaded from UniProt Knowledgebase to convert UniProt IDs to gene symbols and protein names. We didn’t use BioMart for proteins as Ensembl databases only cover about 60-80% protein IDs in a typical proteomics data set. 2.2 Prepare R Data Files by Computational Biologists We recommend uploading csv files, which is convenient for general users who can skip section 2.2 entirely. Nevertheless, experienced R programmers can create R data files to be uploaded through “Upload RData File” option. Section 2.2.1 and 2.2.2 provide example R scripts to prepare such R data files for RNA-Seq and proteomics data, respectively. Two R data files are required for each data set, one contains the main data and the other contains gene co-expression network information. For the pre-loaded datasets, main data files are located in the “data” folder, https://github.com/interactivereport/Quickomics/tree/master/data, and gene co-expression network files are located in the “networkdata” folder, https://github.com/interactivereport/Quickomics/tree/master/networkdata. One can review the content of a R data file (e.g. Mouse_microglia_RNA-Seq.RData) in the “data” folder by loading it into R. The main R data file contains the following R data frame objects. MetaData: It must have “sampleid”, “group”, “Order” and “ComparePairs” columns. Additional metadata columns about samples are optional. “sampleid” should match those used in expression data. “group” holds group names of samples. “Order” is ordered group names used on plotting. “ComparePairs” are names of comparisons performed. ProteinGeneName: It must have “UniqueID”, “Gene.Name” and “Protein.ID” columns. “UniqueID” matches gene ID in below data_wide and data_long objects. “Gene.Name” should be official gene symbols. “Protein.ID” is UniProt protein IDs, or empty for RNA-Seq data. Additional columns about proteins or genes are optional. data_wide: This is the expression matrix in which rows are genes and columns are samples. Samples must match “sampleid” values in MetaData and gene IDs must match “UniqueID” values in ProteinGeneName. data_long: Gene expression matrix in long format with four columns, “UniqueID”, “sampleid”, “expr” and “group”. “group” values must match those listed in MetaData. results_long: The comparison results in long format with five columns, “UniqueID”, “test”, “Adj.P.Value”, “P.Value” and “logFC”. “UniqueID” matches “UniqueID” in ProteinGeneName. “test” column has the comparison names that must match “ComparePairs” values in MetaData. The other values are typically computed from statistical analysis, but the data headers must be changed to “Adj.P.Value”, “P.Value” and “logFC”. data_results: This is a summary table starting with “UniqueID” and “Gene.Name” columns, then the intensity (max or mean expression value from data_wide for each gene), mean and SD expression values for each group, and finally comparison data (comparison name added as prefix of columns). The network data object is computed from “data_wide” expression matrix by using Hmisc R package exemplified by the code snippet below. cor_res <- Hmisc::rcorr(as.matrix(t(data_wide))) cormat <- cor_res$r pmat <- cor_res$P ut <- upper.tri(cormat) network <- tibble::tibble ( from = rownames(cormat)[row(cormat)[ut]], to = rownames(cormat)[col(cormat)[ut]], cor = signif(cormat[ut], 2), p = signif(pmat[ut], 2), direction = as.integer(sign(cormat[ut])) ) 2.2.1 Example R script to prepare R data files from RNA-Seq results We have provided example input files (TPM and count matrix files, sample grouping file, comparison list file) and the R scripts to generate the main data and network R data files at https://github.com/interactivereport/Quickomics/tree/master/demo_files/Example_RNA_Seq_data. Please note that you may need to modify RNA_Seq_raw2quickomics.R to fit your input files. • rsem_TPM.txt: The TPM matrix. One can also use RPKM matrix if needed. • rsem_expected_count.txt: The gene count matrix. We used RSEM counts in this case, but gene count results from other methods can be used as well. • grpID.txt: This file lists the group information for each sample. • comparison.txt: This list lists the comparisons to perform (group 1 vs group 2 in each row). The following command will read the above data files, run differential gene expression analysis using DESeq2, and create main and network R data files. $ Rscript RNA_Seq_raw2quickomics.R 2.2.2 Example R script to prepare R data files from proteomics results We have provided the example input files (normalized protein expression, comparison data, sample information, protein and gene names) and the R script to generate the main data and network R data files at https://github.com/interactivereport/Quickomics/tree/master/demo_files/Example_Proteomics_data. Please note that you may need to modify Proteomics2Quickomics.R to fit your input files. • NormalizedExpression.csv: Normalized protein expression (log2 transformed). • ComparisonData.csv: Comparison results. The statistic values are: logFC, P.Value and Adj.P.Value. This can be created using R packages like limma. • Sample.csv: Sample information file. • ProteinID_Symbol.csv: This file lists the proteinIDs and associate gene symbols. The following command will read the above data files and create main and network R data files. $ Rscript Proteomics2Quickomics.R 2.3 Sample Table A sample table with metadata/details appears upon completion of dataset loading. Here we have selected the “Mouse Microglia RNA” dataset from the previously published paper (Gyoneva et al., 2019) as an example to illustrate all the functionalities. This publication used RNAseq to conclude that the knockout of the Cx3cr1 gene altered the microglial transcriptome in a manner similar to what ageing does, albeit in a milder extent. Using Quickomics, we can visualize the original results from the paper, as well as provide novel visualizations to support new results. The Sample Table contains detailed info of all study samples. A total of 93 samples that were sequenced in this project are listed in the table with attributes like sampleid, group, Age, Genotype and Gender, shown in different columns. 2.4 Project Overview This tab gives an overview of all samples in the project by providing a summary from the metadata. This includes information like which species was used, the different comparisons run and total number of samples in each group. This tab also helps identify how many groups were present in the dataset, like in this project there are 9 different groups that correspond to three genotypes in each of three time points (WT, Het, KO; 2mo, 1yr, 2yr). 2.5 Result Table This tab contains statistical analysis results like Ensemble ID (for RNAseq data) and Accession ID (for proteomics data), gene name, mRNA or protein abundance (count or intensity), mean and SD values for each group, log2 fold change, P value and adjusted P value. 2.6 Data Table The Data table contains normalized expression values (TPM for RNAseq, intensity for label free proteomic quantification, or ratio for isobaric label proteomics quantification) per sample for each gene. This table has a “Download Page” button to download the rows on the current page; to keep the whole table, use “Save to output” (see Chapter 15). 2.7 Protein Gene Names This tab contains all quantified gene or protein IDs and gene names. 2.8 Help Finally, the “Help” feature summarizes what data is being displayed in each tab under Select Dataset. The Help tab is available for all sections of the subsequent analysis.

Chapter 3 Groups and Samples Module 3.1 Overview of the Groups and Samples tab 3.2 Remove groups by sample attributes 3.3 Select and remove multiple samples 3.4 Remove samples by comparisons 3.5 Reorder groups and samples 3.6 Apply changes to all modules

Chapter 3 Groups and Samples Module The “Groups and Samples” module controls which groups, samples and comparisons are used in the rest of Quickomics. It was first introduced in version 2.0 and has been redesigned in the current version. Users can keep or remove samples by any sample attribute (for example group, Age, Genotype or Gender), remove individual samples or comparisons, and re-order groups and samples, all by clicking and dragging buttons in an interactive manner. Changes are made in this tab first, and are passed on to all other modules only after the User clicks “Apply Changes to Project Data”. 3.1 Overview of the Groups and Samples tab The tab is organized from top to bottom as shown below, using the Mouse Microglia RNA dataset (Gyoneva et al., 2019) as an example. At the top, “Reset All” restores the original selection of the project, and “Apply Changes to Project Data” passes the current selection on to all other tabs. The note next to these buttons shows whether the current selection has been applied. The tip below them is a reminder that several buttons can be picked at once with Ctrl + click (Cmd + click on Mac). Next, each categorical sample attribute has its own row. The values that are kept are listed under “Keep (Drag to Order)” and can be dragged to change their order, while values dragged into the “Remove” box on the right are left out. Attributes that are numeric, have only one value, or have a different value for every sample are not shown as rows. In this dataset, the four rows are group, Age, Genotype and Gender. Below the attribute rows, “Available Samples” lists every sample currently included, and “Available Comparisons” lists the comparisons currently included. Individual samples or comparisons can be dragged into the “Drag to Remove Samples” or “Drag to Remove Comparisons” boxes. The line at the bottom summarizes the current selection, here 93 / 93 samples and 9 / 9 comparisons. 3.2 Remove groups by sample attributes To remove all samples sharing an attribute value, drag that value from “Keep” to the “Remove” box of the same row. In the example below, we drag 2yr from the Age row to “Remove” to focus on the 2mo and 1yr microglia. Quickomics updates everything else automatically: the 2yr_Het, 2yr_KO and 2yr_WT groups are moved to “Remove” in the group row, the 2yr samples are moved to “Drag to Remove Samples”, and the four comparisons involving 2yr groups are moved to “Drag to Remove Comparisons”. The summary now shows 64 / 93 samples and 5 / 9 comparisons. The selection is made step by step, so each change starts from the samples currently kept. Dragging a value back to “Keep” adds its samples back, except samples carrying a value that is still removed in another row. The red note “Changes not applied yet. Other tabs still use the previous selection.” is a reminder that the new selection has not been passed on to the other tabs yet (see Section 3.6). 3.3 Select and remove multiple samples Individual samples, for example outliers identified in the QC Plots module, can be removed by dragging them from “Available Samples” to “Drag to Remove Samples”. To move several samples at once, hold Ctrl (Cmd on Mac) and click each sample; the selected samples are outlined in red. Then drag any one of the selected samples, and all of them move together. Here, the three samples 1yr-Het-11M, 1yr-Het-12M and 1yr-Het-14M are moved to “Drag to Remove Samples”. Comparisons that relied on the removed samples are removed as well; in this example 1yr_Hetvs1yr_WT is moved to “Drag to Remove Comparisons”, and the summary shows 61 / 93 samples and 4 / 9 comparisons. Multiple selection works the same way for attribute values and comparisons. 3.4 Remove samples by comparisons Samples can also be selected through the comparisons. When a comparison is dragged from “Available Comparisons” to “Drag to Remove Comparisons”, its samples are removed as well, but only the samples that no remaining comparison uses. In the example below, we remove 2yr_KOvs2yr_WT. The eleven 2yr_KO samples are used only by this comparison, so they are moved to “Drag to Remove Samples”, and the 2yr_KO group is moved to “Remove” in the group row. The 2yr_WT samples are kept, because they are still used by 2yr_Hetvs2yr_WT, 2yr_WTvs1yr_WT and 2yr_WTvs2mo_WT. The summary now shows 82 / 93 samples and 8 / 9 comparisons. Dragging a comparison back to “Available Comparisons” adds its samples back. 3.5 Reorder groups and samples The order of the buttons in each “Keep” box sets the order used in plots and tables. In this example, we drag 2mo in front of 1yr in the Age row, so that the younger animals come first. The groups are re-ordered to 2mo_Het, 2mo_KO, 2mo_WT, 1yr_Het, 1yr_KO, 1yr_WT, and the samples in “Available Samples” follow the new order. Groups, samples and comparisons can also be re-ordered directly by dragging them within their own boxes. Re-ordering comparisons does not change which samples are kept. 3.6 Apply changes to all modules When the selection is final, click “Apply Changes to Project Data”. The note changes to “All changes applied.”, and all other modules (QC Plots, Expression Plot, Heatmap, DEGs and so on) now use the selected groups, samples and comparisons in the selected order.

Chapter 4 QC Plots Module 4.1 PCA Plot 4.2 Covariates 4.3 AlignQC 4.4 Eigenvalues 4.5 PCA 3D Plot 4.6 PCA 3D Interactive 4.7 Sample-sample Distance 4.8 Dendrograms 4.9 Box Plot 4.10 CV Distribution 4.11 Help

Chapter 4 QC Plots Module The “QC Plots” module performs basic QC analyses, as described in following paragraphs, on an uploaded dataset to evaluate integrity and quality of the data. The plots were generated using ggplot, plotly, ComplexHeatmap and pheatmap R packages. All QC plots use the groups, samples and comparisons selected in the “Groups and Samples” module (Chapter 3), and the current selection is shown at the top of the left panel. The width of the left panel can be adjusted with the “Set the Side Menu Width” slider in the upper right corner of the page (15–50% of the page width; the small icon next to it shows or hides the slider). This setting applies to all modules. 4.1 PCA Plot The principle component analysis (PCA) plot displays, by default, the first 2 PC’s in the dataset and colors study groups with “none” selected in shape and size settings. This plot is highly customizable. Users can change the display by annotating the plot with different colors, shapes, size scheme, as well as label selected subsets data points. The PCA settings are shared by the other PCA-based tabs in this module, such as “Eigenvalues”, “PCA 3D Plot” and “PCA 3D Interactive”. To illustrate the strengths of customization, we changed a few display elements as shown below, to visualize the influence of Age and Genotype on sample clustering: We added the Plot/Refresh button to graphs that take time to generate. We also enhanced user interface to show plot progress and display initial plot. In the resulting PCA plot, the 2mo groups separate from the 1yr and 2yr groups, mostly along PC2, which agrees with Age being the factor that drives the biggest separation in this dataset. There is some separation driven by the Genotype as well. Two 2mo_KO samples (2mo-KO-7F and 2mo-KO-8F) lie far from all other samples along PC1. The Ellipsoid feature helps group samples by the color attribute, while the Marginal Rug feature helps understand the sample distribution along the axis. Furthermore, the plot can be saved in high resolution by clicking on “Save to Output”. Chapter 15 of this document describes the next steps of downloading and obtaining the saved plots. 4.2 Covariates The Covariates tab provides flexibility to visualize the covariates, such as Age, group, Genotype showing here. This table contains several columns including the Significance, p-value, and FDR for each covariates listed. Users can also adjust the covariates and cutoffs on the left. 4.3 AlignQC The AlignQC tab contains several sub-tabs to visualize the QC metrics of the alignment step. Here, we can check the ‘Top Gene Ratio’, ‘Top Gene List’, ‘Mapped Read Allocation’, or ‘Plot Other Variables’ across samples. More details can be adjusted on the left panel, such as the height, width, and font size of the plot. The ‘Save to output’ function can add the current plot in the output list. 4.4 Eigenvalues By default, the PCA plot displays PC1 and PC2 as described in Section 4.1. However, in many cases other PC’s may be important in explaining additional variance in the dataset. This sub-tab generates a plot of the variances versus the first 10 PCs in the dataset, enabling Users to make educated decisions of which PCs to plot in 2D scatter plot. In this dataset PC1 and PC2 together explain around 27% of the variance. PC2 and PC3 were used to redo the PCA plot, but here the factors driving the separation of the samples is not as clear. 4.5 PCA 3D Plot This sub-tab contains a way to perform 3D PCA representation. The functionality is limited to doing so only on PC1, PC2 and PC3. Users can zoom in and out to focus on different areas of the plot or rotate the plot in different axes to find the best separation by age as shown below. There are 3 attributes that can be changed: color, ellipsoid inclusion, and labels of the samples. The “Color By” and “Plot Ellipsoid” attributes were changed in the following plot. This highlights the clear separation of samples by Age and not Genotype, contrary to the original biological hypothesis. 4.6 PCA 3D Interactive This tab is similar to the previous one (4.5 PCA 3D Plot), but here users have the additional capability to hover over the samples on the plot to identify more details, see the pointer below. This was implemented through the plotly package in R. Users can change 2 attributes here, the color and shape. In the plot below, the “Color By” and “Shape By” attributes have been changed to highlight the drivers of separation. 4.7 Sample-sample Distance This tab helps identify pair-wise similarity between all samples. It has three sub-tabs: “Distance Heatmap”, “Correlation Heatmap” and “Correlation Data Table”. A short description above each heatmap explains how it is computed. Here again, Users have the option to save the heatmaps to output. The “Distance Heatmap” shows the Euclidean distance between every sample pair, computed from the expression values. Smaller distances mean that two samples have more similar overall expression profiles. By default, the rows and columns are clustered based on similarity; this can be turned off with “Apply Clustering”. It is clear from this plot that samples of the same Age have the smaller distances, that is, they have closer gene expression patterns. The “Correlation Heatmap” shows the correlation between every sample pair. Unlike the distance, the correlation is scale-invariant, so it highlights shared expression patterns rather than absolute differences in expression. Users can choose how the samples are annotated (“Annotate By”) and labeled (“Axis Label By”), and whether to apply clustering. Selecting “Yes” under “Show More Options” gives further control over the heatmap colors, the colors of the annotations (set automatically by a random seed, selected from palettes, or uploaded as a csv file), font sizes and plot height. In this example, the samples are annotated by Age, and samples of the same Age are highly correlated with each other. The “Correlation Data Table” lists the correlation values of all sample pairs in a searchable table, which can be downloaded by page or as a whole. 4.8 Dendrograms Like the previous plot (4.7 Sample-sample Distance), the Dendrogram plot helps visualize hierarchical clustering relationships between samples. The Default plot is Circular and cut into four parts. Users have the option to visualize in two other ways (tree or horizontal) and cut the plot in multiple regions. Here again, Users can save the plot to output. In the plot below, we have selected to visualize as a tree and cut into eight parts. This shows the relationship between the samples to help understand the hierarchal clustering. Overall, the samples are arranged by age, but there are some outliers that appear. The 2mo samples form their own branches, while the 2yr samples cluster together with part of the 1yr samples. 4.9 Box Plot The Boxplot is a visualization to understand the distribution of the normalized expression levels in all samples. This identifies the minimum, first quartile, median, third quartile, and maximum values in the dataset. In this demo dataset, most of the samples have the same range of expression, indicating that there are no outliers. 4.10 CV Distribution This plot shows the histogram of CVs (coefficient of variation) and a dotted line for each group indicates the median CV. In this dataset, the 2mo_KO samples have the highest CV while the 2yr_Het samples have the lowest variability, which corresponds to what is visually seen on the PCA plot for these samples in Section 4.1. 4.11 Help The Help section describes each tab of the QC Plot and what is being visualized. For further help please visit the GitHub containing the source code for this tools (https://github.com/interactivereport/Quickomics) or click on the link at the bottom of the page.

Chapter 5 DEG Module 5.1 DEG Counts 5.2 Volcano Plot (Static) 5.3 Volcano Plot (Interactive) 5.4 DEGs and DEPs in Two Comparisons 5.5 Data Table

Chapter 5 DEG Module This section is designed to explore the differentially expressed genes (DEGs) and differentially expressed proteins (DEPs) in the dataset. The comparisons are defined by the User when they input the dataset. Please refer to our GitHub for more details on uploading datasets. The “Volcano Plot (Static)” described in Section 5.2 and “Volcano Plot (Interactive)” described in Section 5.3 are ways to visualize each pair-wise comparison one by one. “DEGs/DEPs in Two Comparisons” described in Section 5.4 is a novel way to visualize the similarities and differences in two comparisons. Finally, “Data Table” described in Section 5.5 displays a searchable table containing all genes and their fold changes and P values in each comparison. 5.1 DEG Counts The DEG Counts tab provides a summary of the number of significantly changed genes for each comparison, separating Up- and Down-regulated genes. 5.2 Volcano Plot (Static) This plot reveals the differentially expressed genes provided in the input data file. By default, the Fold change Cutoff is set to 1.2 and the P value Cutoff is set to 0.01. Users have the option to change any of these parameters. For more advanced display options, they can set the “Show More Options” to “Yes” to customize other settings. The red dots are indicative of all genes that pass the Fold Change and P value cutoff, while the green dots are indicative of genes that only pass the P value cutoff. By default, the DEGs with the largest fold changes are labeled, up to 50 genes. In the example below, we selected the 2mo_Hetvs2mo_WT comparison with the default parameters; 82 genes pass the cutoffs, 21 up- and 61 down-regulated. For demonstration purposes, we have changed the following attributes to highlight a few genes in this dataset. We kept the 2mo_Hetvs2mo_WT comparison and the default cutoffs. In the example below, we select an “Immune Response” dataset from the Molecular Signatures Database (MSigDB) to highlight the genes by adding labels to the volcano plot. As MSigDB contains only human gene lists and the demo dataset is from mouse, Quickomics does a quick conversion of the names of Human genes to Mouse genes by changing the letters after the first one to lowercase. The genes of the selected gene set are listed in the box below the “Select Geneset” button, where genes can be added or removed. If the list contains more genes than the number set by “# of Genes to Label” (50 by default), only that many are labeled. The label color can be changed with “Gene Label Color”. Of the labeled immune genes, Cfp is among the most strongly down-regulated genes, while most of the others are not significantly changed in 2mo Het microglia. A set of genes can also be shown in a different color. Select “Yes” under “Highlight a Set of Genes in a Different Color?”, enter the genes to highlight, choose their color, and enter the genes from this list that should be labeled; genes entered in the label box are always labeled. Then click “Apply Highlight”. The highlight list and labels work separately from “Label Genes”, so in the example below we set “Label Genes” to “None” and highlighted five genes that are significantly changed in the 1yr_Hetvs1yr_WT comparison: Prkcq, Unc13b, Galnt6, Phldb1 and Gm32591. In 2mo_Hetvs2mo_WT, none of them pass the cutoffs, so they are among the grey dots. Genes can also be sent to this list from the interactive volcano plot (Section 5.3). Under “Show More Options”, “Rasterize plot” draws the dots as a bitmap image while keeping the text and axes sharp, which makes saved plots smaller when there are many genes. 5.3 Volcano Plot (Interactive) This next sub-tab is a very similar visualization as the previous one (5.2 Volcano Plot (Static)) with an additional capability where users can hover over a particular dot/gene on the plot to see more details. This plot has a few attributes that can be changed, and in the example below we have used the same cutoffs as in Section 5.2. Genes can also be selected directly on the plot. Choose the lasso or box-select tool in the toolbar at the top right of the plot and circle a group of dots; the number of selected genes and a table of these genes (with their logFC, P value and adjusted P value) appear below the plot, and the table can be downloaded as CSV or Excel. Double-clicking the plot clears the selection. Clicking “Send Selected Genes to Highlight List” copies the selected genes to the highlight list of the static volcano plot (Section 5.2), where they can be shown in a different color after clicking “Apply Highlight”. In the example below, 76 strongly down-regulated genes in 2mo_KOvs2mo_WT were selected. 5.4 DEGs and DEPs in Two Comparisons This next tab helps with identifying DEGs/DEPs that follow a similar trend in two comparisons. Gyoneva et al., 2019, the source of this demo dataset, report that the genes differentially expressed in Cx3cr1 KO microglia in the 2mo KO are quite different from WT, while the differences from WT are smaller for the 1yr KO and 2yr KO, and the two older ages are similar to each other. We have plotted out the following comparisons that illustrate this conclusion. 2mo_KOvs2mo_WT vs 1yr_KOvs1yr_WT has a low correlation score of 0.211. There are many genes that are colored orange, meaning those genes were significant in 2mo_KOvs2mo_WT (Y axis) but not in 1yr_KOvs1yr_WT (X axis). Similarly, we changed the X axis to 2yr_KOvs2yr_WT to compare to 2mo_KOvs2mo_WT, and it shows a very similar plot with a low correlation score of 0.178. Next, we changed the Y axis comparison to 1yr_KOvs1yr_WT comparing it to 2yr_KOvs2yr_WT on the X axis. This plot has a higher correlation score of 0.348 than the previous one, suggesting that these two comparisons are more similar. These comparisons represent additional insights supported by statistical analyses that were gained from the data and were not available in the original manuscript by Gyoneva et al. Under “Show More Options”, “Color DEGs using dot color?” sets whether the gene labels take the color of their dots (“Yes”) or are all drawn in one color (“No”). 5.5 Data Table This tab lets the users view the DEGs/DEPs in a tabular format with a searchable feature. Users also have the ability to download the gene list as a CSV.

Chapter 6 Heatmap Module 6.1 Static Heatmap Layout 1 6.2 Static Heatmap Layout 2 6.3 Interactive Heatmap

Chapter 6 Heatmap Module This module generates highly customized publication-quality heatmaps with the ComplexHeatmap package in R. Users can enter automated list of differentially expressed genes or enter a custom list of genes to highlight on the heatmap. This module differs from other modules in that each time Users change the attributes; they need to click on the “Plot/Refresh” button to generate the plot. This is to avoid changing the output before all the attribute are added. 6.1 Static Heatmap Layout 1 The “Static Heatmap Layout 1” uses the ComplexHeatmap package (Gu et al., 2016) for generating the plot. For demo purposes, we have selected options that highlight some capabilities to generate informative heatmap. For gene selection the default option is the selection of 100 random genes which can also be changed to variable genes. Here we selected DEGs/DEPs from the 2yr_WTvs2mo_WT comparison. Users also have the option to change the cutoff criteria for filtering the genes. They can also add/remove annotation categories for the samples on the columns. In the example below, we used a Fold Change Cutoff of 2, which gives 464 genes, annotated the samples with Age, Gender and Genotype, and set “Reorder Samples by Annotation Attributes?” to “Yes”. The samples are then sorted by Age first, then by Gender and then by Genotype, instead of being clustered. In this heatmap, the top up-regulated genes in 2mo_WT samples are seen as high in 2mo samples but low in 2yr and 1yr samples, while the top up-regulated genes in the 2yr_WT samples are high in the 2yr and 1yr samples but low in the 2mo samples. Because the samples are grouped by Age, these blocks are easy to see. This is another example that age has a major effect on gene expression in microglia, and the 2mo microglia have a different gene expression profile compared to 1yr and 2yr. In this next example, we customize another heatmap. We selected genes from the 2mo_KOvs2mo_WT comparison and raised the Fold Change Cutoff to 1.43, which gives 236 genes. We limited the sample annotations to Age and Genotype, set “Reorder Samples by Annotation Attributes?” to “No” so that the samples are clustered, and changed the font sizes. Under “Show More Options”, we changed the Low, Mid and High colors and set “cutree_rows” to 4, so the genes are cut into 4 parts. 6.2 Static Heatmap Layout 2 The “Static Heatmap Layout 2” uses the heatmap.2 function from the gplots package for generating the plot. Here is a demo with 100 random genes with dendrograms for both rows and columns. 6.3 Interactive Heatmap The “Interactive Heatmap” tab shows the selected genes in Morpheus, a heatmap viewer that runs in the browser and has no limit on the number of genes. Click “Plot/Refresh” to draw the heatmap. In the example below, we used the same 464 genes from 2yr_WTvs2mo_WT as in Section 6.1, and the line above the heatmap shows “464 rows by 93 columns”. The menus above the heatmap (File, Edit, View, Tools and Help) and the toolbar offer many functions; for example, “View → Fit To Window” shows all genes and samples at once, the search box finds genes (with “Rows” selected) or samples (with “Columns” selected), and the “Tools” menu offers clustering, sorting, filtering and other analyses. “Click to view Interactive Heatmap Guide” opens a short guide with a link to the Morpheus tutorial, which describes these functions in detail. The tutorial uses its own example data, so its steps for opening data files can be skipped; in Quickomics the data are loaded automatically.
expression-plot-module.html
Chapter 7 Expression Plot Module 7.1 Browsing 7.2 Searched Expression Data 7.3 Data Table 7.4 Result Table 7.5 Rank Abundance Curve

Chapter 7 Expression Plot Module This functional module allows Users to browse through a subset of genes/proteins. It also offers an option to plot expression of individually selected genes. Four different displays: Box Plot, Bar Plot, Violin Plot and Line Plot are made available to fit the Users’ preference. In Quickomics v2.0, we enhanced the Expression Plot module: Genes can be ranked by p-value or logFC, and the number of columns in the graph can be changed. 7.1 Browsing This tab lets the Users plot out the expression of the DEGs/DEPs identified in the different comparisons. In this example below, we demonstrate how to display a few top genes as Violin Plots. 7.2 Searched Expression Data Another way to plot genes/proteins is using this functionality. Users can either enter a custom list of genes/proteins or select a list from online databases like KEGG, MSigDB etc. The selected genes/proteins can be plotted on a single plot or in multiple plots. Here is an example of plotting genes involved in MHCII antigen processing. The resulting plot shows the expression of a subset of genes from the MHCII antigen presentation family of genes. Many of them appear altered by gene KO in 2mon microglia, but also in all genotypes in 2yr microglia, as indicated in the publication. 7.3 Data Table This sub-tab lists the normalized data of the genes/proteins selected in “Searched Expression Data” (Section 7.2) as a searchable table. For a demo of this feature, we select a proteome dataset from published paper (Connor-Robson et al., 2019). Once the dataset is selected, we go into the “Searched Expression Data” sub-tab to select a gene set. Finally, we click the “Data Table” tab to look at the expression of the protein selected for a searchable table of values. 7.4 Result Table This tab lists the statistics results of the genes/proteins selected in “Searched Expression Data” as a searchable table. Each comparison defined is probed for the genes in the list and the P value and Fold changes are listed. This is specifically designed for the gene values, unlike “Data Table” in the previous section (7.3) that is designed for protein values. 7.5 Rank Abundance Curve This functionality helps identify the relative abundance of a list of genes within a dataset. This plot helps interpret the distribution of abundance and expression levels of a set of genes. A steep gradient indicates the genes are very different in their expression levels as the high-ranking species have much higher abundances than the low-ranking species. A shallow gradient indicates that the genes have very similar expression levels as the abundances of different species are similar.

Chapter 8 Gene Set Enrichment Module 8.1 Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA) 8.2 Over-Representation Analysis (ORA) 8.3 Gene Expression 8.4 Gene Set Heat Map 8.5 KEGG Pathway View 8.6 WikiPathways View 8.7 Dot Plot

Chapter 8 Gene Set Enrichment Module This functionality in Quickomics is an extension to the differential gene identification. Users are able to use different cutoffs to filter out DEGs/DEPs in different comparisons and probe enriched pathways. This is a useful way to make biological sense of the data. We also improved the robustness of Gene Set Enrichment Module in Quickomics v2.0, using human gene set enrichment for unknown species instead of giving error. The updated system performs more error checking and data cleanup in the backend. In the current version, the module offers two enrichment methods, Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA, Section 8.1) and Over-Representation Analysis (ORA, Section 8.2), and several views of the results: Gene Expression (8.3), Gene Set Heatmap (8.4), KEGG Pathway View (8.5), WikiPathways View (8.6) and Dot Plot (8.7). Multiple comparisons can be supported. 8.1 Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA) The “Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA)” tab tests whether the genes of a gene set change together in a comparison. Unlike ORA (Section 8.2), which uses only the genes passing the cutoffs, GSEA ranks all genes of a comparison by logFC or by -log(P-Value) and tests whether the genes of a gene set are found at the top or bottom of the ranked list. Select the comparison(s), the ranking method, the gene set size range, the adjusted P-value cutoff and the gene set collections, then click “Compute/Refresh”. In the results table, a positive normalized enrichment score (NES) means that the gene set is up-regulated, and a negative NES means that it is down-regulated. The “Copy Leading Edge Genes” button copies the genes that drive the enrichment, so that they can be pasted into other modules. Clicking a gene set name in the GSEA or ORA results table selects it for the Gene Expression, Gene Set Heatmap, KEGG Pathway View and WikiPathways View tabs. To demonstrate usage of this functionality, we will use the Mouse Microglia RNA dataset to help answer the question which pathways were altered by Genotype and/or Age. Very similar to the results from Gyoneva et al., 2019, this analysis points to immune related terms being down-regulated in 2mo_KOvs2mo_WT. In the example below for 2mo_KOvs2mo_WT, complement and coagulation cascades and viral protein interaction with cytokine and cytokine receptor have negative NES values; the same pathways are also found by ORA in the down-regulated genes (Section 8.2). 8.2 Over-Representation Analysis (ORA) The “Over-Representation Analysis (ORA)” tab tests whether the DEGs/DEPs of a comparison are over-represented in gene sets. Users pick one or more comparisons, apply cutoff criteria, choose up-, down- or both-regulated genes, and select the gene set collections; then click “Compute/Refresh” to run the analysis. Gene sets are available for human, mouse and rat. When the gene sets come from another species than the project, “Gene Symbol Mapping” converts the gene symbols, for example by homologous genes. In the example below, we used the same comparison, 2mo_KOvs2mo_WT, with human KEGG pathways with homologous gene mapping, a Fold Change Cutoff of 1.43 and a P value cutoff of 0.01; the top down-regulated pathways include cytokine-cytokine receptor interaction, viral protein interaction with cytokine and cytokine receptor, complement and coagulation cascades, and hematopoietic cell lineage. Similarly, we select the up-regulated genes. Four KEGG pathways are enriched: rheumatoid arthritis, antigen processing and presentation, fluid shear stress and atherosclerosis, and leishmaniasis. 8.3 Gene Expression For the enriched terms identified in the GSEA (Section 8.1) or ORA (Section 8.2) tab, Users have the ability to look at the differential values of the genes present in the set. Click a gene set name in the ORA or GSEA results table, then open the “Gene Expression” tab. It shows the statistics of the gene set and lists all genes in the set with their logFC, P value and adjusted P value; the DE genes used in the ORA are shown in green. Here we are probing hsa04061 Viral protein interaction with cytokine and cytokine receptor, identified in the down-regulated category; 7 of its 42 genes, such as CX3CR1, CCR2 and CCR5, are down-regulated DE genes. 8.4 Gene Set Heat Map Like the “Gene Expression” tab, Users have the ability to plot expression of the genes in the pathway term selected as a heatmap. This visualization shows that while the genes of the cytokine-cytokine receptor interaction pathway are enriched in the down-regulated genes, not all of them change in the same direction across the groups. 8.5 KEGG Pathway View This functionality is available only to KEGG pathway terms. Users have the option to view the Fold Change levels of different genes in the KEGG pathway selected for one or more comparisons. In this example we demo the KEGG pathway “hsa04612 Antigen processing and presentation” for the 2mo_KOvs2mo_WT and 1yr_KOvs1yr_WT comparisons. Each gene box shows one color per comparison. This figure identifies all the genes that are differentially expressed in this pathway. Most genes in the MHC I pathway change little, while CD74 in the MHC II pathway is down-regulated in both comparisons. The visualization is also useful to highlight whether or not a large proportion of genes in a pathway are altered by the perturbation. 8.6 WikiPathways View This tab shows the logFC values of the selected comparison on a WikiPathways diagram. Select a pathway by clicking its name in the ORA or GSEA results table, or choose it from the “Wikipathways for Visualization” list. The colors for low, middle and high logFC values and the log2FC range can be changed in the left panel. In the example below, we show the Microglia pathogen phagocytosis pathway (WP3937) for 2mo_KOvs2mo_WT; up-regulated genes are shown in red and down-regulated genes in green. 8.7 Dot Plot The Dot Plot compares the enrichment results of several comparisons in one figure. First run GSEA or ORA for the comparisons of interest and choose the same “Analysis Type” in the left panel. The comparisons to plot can be re-ordered or removed by dragging them. Choose how the top gene sets are selected (from each comparison separately, from all comparisons together, or from a customized list) and the total number of gene sets, then click “Plot/Refresh”. The table above the plot lists how many of the plotted gene sets come from each comparison. The dot color shows the NES (GSEA) and the dot size shows -log10 of the adjusted P value. In the example below, we ran GSEA for 2mo_KOvs2mo_WT, 1yr_KOvs1yr_WT and 2yr_KOvs2yr_WT and plotted the top 30 KEGG pathways.

Chapter 9 Pattern Clustering Module 9.1 Clustering of Centroid Profiles 9.2 Data Table

Chapter 9 Pattern Clustering Module This functional module in Quickomics helps cluster genes/proteins based on their expression profiles across different groups. Three different algorithms, soft (fuzzy) clustering, k-means and partitioning around medoids (PAM), are implemented. 9.1 Clustering of Centroid Profiles Users have the option to either select the DEGs/DEPS as the list of genes/proteins to cluster based off on or upload a custom gene list. DEGs/DEPs can be selected from one comparison or from all comparisons, and cutoffs can be applied to limit the number of genes. Users also choose the sample attribute to plot, how the expression values are transformed before clustering (“Cluster On”, described in the guide above the plot), and the order of the groups; then click “Plot/Refresh”. In this example below, we select the DEGs/DEPs from all comparisons with a Fold Change cutoff of 3 and a P value cutoff of 0.01, which gives 177 genes, and identify 6 clusters of genes. Please note that this visualization for this dataset is novel and was not previously reported in Gyoneva et al., 2019. The genes in each cluster can be viewed in the “Data Table” tab. 9.2 Data Table The data table contains genes from the previous clusters, along with their gene names and the values used for clustering, here the z-scores of the group means; the “cluster” column gives the cluster number shown in the previous tab. The layout of the table is set by “Data Output Format” in the left panel. By default, the table is shown in the wide format: each gene is shown in one row, the values of the groups are in separate columns, from 2mo_WT to 2yr_KO, followed by the cluster number. In the long format, each gene is shown in one row per group. In this example there are nine groups, so each gene appears in nine rows, and the table has 1,593 rows for the 177 genes. Each row gives the group, the gene, the “mean” column with the mean expression of the gene in that group, the “value” column with the z-score used for clustering, and the cluster number. For example, Clec10a has a mean expression of 3.33 in 2mo_WT and 1.38 in 2yr_WT; after the z-score transformation these become 1.69 and -0.391, and the gene belongs to cluster 2, the genes that are high in the 2mo groups and low in the 1yr and 2yr groups. The long format is useful when the table is downloaded to make plots or to filter the data in other software.

Chapter 10 Correlation Network Module 10.1 visNetwork 10.2 Data Table

Chapter 10 Correlation Network Module This module helps build co-expression networks based on gene-gene or protein-protein correlations. This is especially useful during co-immunoprecipitation or pulldown proteomics experiments to identify protein partners. Users have the ability to enter 1 or more genes/proteins to identify if their expression is correlated. 10.1 visNetwork This uses the R package visNetwork to visualize the expression of correlated genes/proteins. Users have the ability to choose the R and P value cutoff for selecting the correlated genes/proteins. In this example below, we probe 3 genes and identify the expression of other genes that are correlated with them. The following network plot was produced. Gnai3 is part of a large network with multiple genes correlated with it. On the other hand, Klf6 was correlated with 2 other genes, while Btbd17 was not correlated with any genes. 10.2 Data Table The genes identified in the previous tab as part of the network plot are available as a table in this tab. Users can perform searches and sort based on correlation statistics.

Chapter 11 Venn Diagram Module 11.1 Venn Diagram 11.2 Venn Diagram (black & white) 11.3 Intersection Output 11.4 DEG Table

Chapter 11 Venn Diagram Module This module in Quickomics helps Users identify DEGs/DEPs that are common or unique to different comparisons within one project. Users have the option to either visualize these DEGs/DEPs as a highly customizable Venn Diagram or download a table with the gene names. 11.1 Venn Diagram To view the DEGs/DEPs as a Venn Diagram, Users have the option to see the intersection of DEGs/DEPs for up to 5 different comparisons. Users can also use all DEGs/DEPs or restrict it to the ones that are Up or Down regulated. In this example there were 33 DEGs that were identified in the three comparisons probed here, which represent the set of genes altered by the KO genotype at each of the time points. 11.2 Venn Diagram (black & white) This tab has the same plot seen before in Section 11.1 but highly simplified and in black and white. 11.3 Intersection Output This tab lets the User view the individual genes that were present in the Venn Diagram and the distribution of the genes in intersection regions. 11.4 DEG Table This tab lets the Users view the Fold Change and p value of the genes identified in the Venn Diagram in the comparisons being queried.
wgcna-module.html
Chapter 12 WGCNA Module 12.1 WGCNA QC 12.2 WGCNA Result 12.3 Module Eigengenes 12.4 Module-Trait Relationships

Chapter 12 WGCNA Module Weighted Gene Co-expression Network Analysis (WGCNA) finds groups of genes, called modules, whose expression goes up and down together across the samples. Genes in the same module often work in the same biological process. Each module is summarized by its eigengene, a single profile that represents the expression of all genes of the module, and the eigengenes can be correlated with sample attributes such as Age or Genotype to find the modules linked to them. WGCNA takes a long time to compute, so Quickomics loads pre-computed results when a project has them. For the Mouse Microglia demo dataset, the results were pre-computed with the 10,000 most variable genes and a Dendrogram Cut Height for Merging of 0.25, and they are shown as soon as the WGCNA tab is opened. Users can change the number of genes or the cut height in the left panel and click “Run” to compute new results; this can take 3–10 minutes. The tabs are described below in the order of a typical analysis: WGCNA QC (Section 12.1), WGCNA Result (12.2), Module Eigengenes (12.3) and Module-Trait Relationships (12.4). Each tab has a green link that opens a short guide, and the “Help” tab describes the whole workflow. 12.1 WGCNA QC Before the network is built, WGCNA raises the correlations between genes to a power, called the soft-thresholding power. A higher power keeps the strong correlations and pushes the weak ones toward zero. The “Soft-Thresholding Power” sub-tab shows how well the network fits a scale-free topology (SFT.R.sq) and the mean connectivity of the genes for each power. The usual choice is the lowest power with an R² above 0.8, which is marked by the red line in the Scale Independence plot. For the demo dataset, power 6 is the first power above this line, with an R² of 0.906 and a mean connectivity of 301, and it is highlighted in the table as the power used. 12.2 WGCNA Result The “Dendrogram Plot” sub-tab shows how the genes are clustered by their co-expression. The colored bar below the tree shows the module of each gene: genes of the same module share a color, and grey genes are not assigned to any module. Modules whose eigengenes are very similar are merged; a lower “Dendrogram Cut Height for Merging” keeps more, smaller modules. The “Gene Cluster Summary Table” sub-tab lists each module with its number of genes and the genes it contains. In the demo dataset there are six modules plus 4,238 grey genes, with sizes from 79 genes in the red module to 2,569 genes in the turquoise module. For each module, “Copy all genes” copies its genes so that they can be pasted into other modules of Quickomics, and “Run ORA” runs Over-Representation Analysis on its genes (see Section 8.2). For example, the yellow module includes Xist and Tsix. “Save GCT data file to output” saves the expression data with the module of each gene, which can be downloaded from the Output module (Chapter 15). 12.3 Module Eigengenes The “Eigengene table” sub-tab lists the eigengene value of every module in every sample. The “Eigengene Network” sub-tab shows how the modules relate to each other. In the tree at the top, modules with similar eigengenes are joined at a lower height; in the heatmap below, red means that two eigengenes are similar and blue means they are not. In the demo dataset, the blue and brown modules are joined first, and the red module is close to them. 12.4 Module-Trait Relationships The “Module Trait Heatmap” sub-tab correlates the eigengene of each module with the sample attributes. Select the attributes, choose a base level for each, and click “Plot Module Trait Correlation”. Each level of an attribute becomes one column of the heatmap; red cells mean that the module is higher in the samples of that level, and blue cells mean that it is lower. Hovering over a cell shows the correlation and its P value. In the example below, we selected Age, Genotype and Gender. The blue module has the strongest correlation, 0.94 with Age2mo, so its genes are higher in the 2mo samples. The green module shows the opposite pattern, with a correlation of −0.87 with Age2mo and 0.79 with Age2yr. As in the earlier chapters, Age has a much larger effect than Genotype, and the yellow module, which includes Xist and Tsix, is correlated with GenderF. Hub genes are the most connected genes of a module and are often key genes of the process it represents. In the “Hub Gene Identification Table” sub-tab, select a trait and optionally a module, then click “Run”. For each gene, the table lists its connectivity within the module, its module membership (the correlation of the gene with the module eigengene) and its gene significance (the correlation of the gene with the trait), with their P values. In the example below, we selected the trait Age2mo and the blue module. The 895 genes are sorted by connectivity, and the top hub genes include several histone genes, such as Hist1h2ac, Hist4h4 and Hist1h3e. The “Hub Gene Identification Plot” sub-tab shows the same results as two plots. The left plot compares the module membership and the gene significance of each gene; in the blue module they are highly correlated (cor = 0.968), which means that the genes most central to the module are also the most related to Age2mo. The right plot shows the connectivity of each gene against its module membership, and the top 10% most connected genes, the hub genes, are shown in red.
time-course-analysis-module.html
Chapter 13 Time Course Analysis Module 13.1 Time-Series DE Analysis 13.2 DEG Clustering Analysis 13.3 Similar Pattern Search

Chapter 13 Time Course Analysis Module This module finds genes whose expression changes over time, groups them by the shape of their time pattern, and finds genes that follow the same pattern as a gene of interest. Any sample attribute with ordered levels can be used as the time variable. The Mouse Microglia demo dataset has no real time series, but its three ages (2mo, 1yr and 2yr) can be used as time points, with Genotype as the condition. The module has three tabs, described below: Time-Series DE Analysis (Section 13.1), DEG Clustering Analysis (13.2) and Similar Pattern Search (13.3). Each tab has a green link that opens a short guide to its method. 13.1 Time-Series DE Analysis Select the time variable and, optionally, one or more condition variables, then choose the method and the test and click “Run Time-Series DE Analysis”. Two methods are offered: DESeq2 for RNA-seq data and limma for continuous log values such as proteomics data; the default is chosen from the expression unit of the project. Two tests are offered. “Time x Condition” finds genes whose trend over time is different between the conditions, and “Time only” finds genes that change over time. Unlike the DEG module, the P values describe the whole trend of a gene, not a single fold change between two groups. In the example below, we used Age as the time variable, Genotype as the condition and the Time x Condition test, so the analysis asks which genes change with age differently in Het, KO and WT microglia. 169 genes pass the adjusted P value cutoff of 0.05. The max_time_log2FC columns give, for each genotype, the log2 fold change between the time points with the highest and the lowest mean expression. For the top gene, Mmp8, this value is 3.75 in WT but only 0.26 in Het and 0.25 in KO, so Mmp8 changes strongly over time in WT but hardly at all in the other two genotypes. The table can be saved with “Save to output”. 13.2 DEG Clustering Analysis This tab groups the significant genes from Section 13.1 into clusters of genes with the same time pattern. Set the “Minimum Genes per Cluster” and click “Run Clustering”; smaller clusters are left out, so this number may need to be lowered when there are few significant genes. The “Time Series Cluster Plot” sub-tab shows one panel per cluster, with the number of genes in its title. For each genotype, the box plots show the expression of the genes in the cluster at each age, scaled as z-scores, and the line shows the trend. Note that the plot gives the ages in years, so 2mo is shown as 0.164yr. In the example below, 102 of the 169 genes fall into three clusters of 35, 19 and 48 genes. In all three clusters, the genes are much higher in 2mo WT samples than at the later ages, while Het and KO show smaller changes. The “DEG Cluster Result” sub-tab lists the genes of each cluster. “Copy all genes” copies them so they can be pasted into other modules, and “Create Expression Plot” shows their expression in the Expression Plot module (Chapter 7). The “Time-series Sample Heatmap” and “Time-series Group Heatmap” sub-tabs show the genes of the clusters as heatmaps, one column per sample or one column per group. Click “Plot/Refresh” to draw the heatmap after changing the settings. In the group heatmap below, the columns are the three ages within each genotype, and the rows are the genes, split by cluster. The high values in the 2mo column of WT stand out in all three clusters. The data behind each heatmap can be saved as a GCT file with the buttons above it. 13.3 Similar Pattern Search This tab finds genes whose expression changes over time in the same way as a chosen gene, or in the opposite way. Run the Time-Series DE Analysis first, then type a gene in “Gene to Match”, choose whether to search among all tested genes or only among the significant genes, and click “Find Similar Genes”. The plot shows the mean expression of the chosen gene, the seed gene, as a red dashed line, together with the most similar genes, for each condition and time point. The table ranks the genes by how well their pattern matches the seed gene (kendall_r and pearson_r, where 1 is a perfect match); change_distance shows how close the size of the changes is, with smaller values meaning closer to the seed gene, and DE_padj gives the adjusted P value of the gene from Section 13.1. In the example below, we searched all tested genes for genes similar to Mmp8. The top genes, such as 1500015O10Rik, Kcnj13, Sell and Chil3, are also high in 2mo WT samples and change little in Het and KO. “Copy seed + selected genes” and “Create Expression Plot” pass the genes to other modules, and the plot and table can be saved to the output.
correlation-analysis-module.html
Chapter 14 Correlation Analysis Module 14.1 Gene-Gene, Sample-Sample and Group-Group 14.2 Gene-Target

Chapter 14 Correlation Analysis Module This module measures how closely two things change together across the samples. Four types of correlation are offered under “Correlation Type”. Gene-Gene, Sample-Sample and Group-Group correlate each pair of the selected genes, samples or groups (Section 14.1). Gene-Target correlates every gene with one target, which can be a gene or a sample attribute such as Age (Section 14.2). To see the correlation of all samples at once, use the sample correlation heatmap in the QC Plots module (Chapter 4). Each tab has a green link that opens a short guide. 14.1 Gene-Gene, Sample-Sample and Group-Group Select the correlation type and the genes, samples or groups to compare, choose Pearson for linear relationships or Spearman for relationships that go in one direction but need not be linear, and click “Compute/Refresh”. Genes can be selected by name, browsed, entered as a list with “Upload Genes”, or taken from a gene set. The “Result Table” lists every pair with its correlation, R squared and P value, ranked from the strongest correlation. In the example below, we entered the MHC class II genes H2-Aa, H2-Ab1, H2-Eb1 and Cd74 together with Cx3cr1. The MHC class II genes are highly correlated with each other, with correlations from 0.91 to 0.98, while their correlations with Cx3cr1 are lower, between 0.55 and 0.66. Clicking “View Correlation Plot” in a row opens the “Correlation Plot” tab with the scatter plot of that pair. Each dot is a sample, and the plot shows the correlation, the regression line and its equation, and the P value. Below is the plot for H2-Aa and H2-Ab1, with a correlation of 0.980. The “Data Table” tab lists the values used. Sample-Sample and Group-Group correlations are set up in the same way, by selecting at least two samples, or an attribute and at least two of its groups. 14.2 Gene-Target Gene-Target correlates every gene with one target across the individual samples, to find the genes that go up and down with it. The target can be a gene or a sample attribute. Numeric attributes, such as a dose or a score, are used as they are. For text levels with an order, choose “Ordered levels” and list the levels from lowest to highest; Spearman correlation is then used. Because the ages of the demo dataset are given in different units (2mo, 1yr and 2yr), the app uses “Ordered levels” for Age, and we put the levels in the order 2mo, 1yr, 2yr. After clicking “Compute/Refresh”, the table lists all 15,402 genes sorted by their correlation with Age. Crlf2, St14, Mageh1 and H2-Q6 have the highest correlations, above 0.93, while genes such as Gm10616 and Ctf2 have negative correlations, so they decrease with age. The samples can also be limited to some levels of an attribute with “Restrict samples to”. The table can be saved with “Save table to output”. Clicking a row in the table shows the gene in the “Gene-Target Plot” tab. Each dot is a sample, and the line shows the trend. Crlf2 increases steadily from 2mo to 1yr to 2yr, with a Spearman correlation of 0.94. With “Compute separately for each level of”, the correlation is computed separately within each level of another attribute, and the table gets one set of columns per level. The “Correlation Heatmap” tab then shows the correlations of the top genes, one column per level, with red for positive and blue for negative correlations; the number of genes is set with “Top genes to show”. In the example below, we computed the correlation with Age separately for each genotype. The top 30 genes have the same direction in Het, KO and WT, so their change with age does not depend on the genotype.

Chapter 15 Output Module 15.1 Save Session

Chapter 15 Output Module This final tab in Quickomics is available for Users to download plots in high resolution, including for use in publications. Users can save different plots by clicking on “Save to Output” present on the top left corner of the plot during analysis and exploration of the datasets in all previous tabs. Upon clicking on the “Output” tab as seen in the image below, Users can see a list of plots that are available to download to their local machine. Tables and heatmap data can be saved in the same way. Tables saved with “Save to output”, for example the DEG data table, are listed under “Tables to Save” and are downloaded together as one Excel (.xlsx) file. Heatmap data saved with “Save GCT data file to output” in the Heatmap module (Chapter 6) are listed under “GCT tables to Save” and are downloaded as GCT files, which can be opened in other tools such as Morpheus. In the example below, we saved the PCA plot, a volcano plot and a heatmap, the DEG data table, and the heatmap data. 15.1 Save Session “Save Session” saves the current settings of all tabs, such as the selected groups and samples, comparisons, cutoffs and plot options, so that the same analysis can be continued later. Click “Save Session”, then click “Download Session File” to download the settings as a file; the file name starts with the project name, for example Mouse_microglia_RNA-Seq_20261105_124611.rds. To continue later, open the same project and upload the file under “Restore Session from File”; Quickomics then restores the settings of all tabs. A session file can only be restored in the project it was saved from. Only the settings are saved: plots and tables saved to the Output tab are not included in the session file, so they have to be saved again after the session is restored.

Chapter 16 FAQ

Chapter 16 FAQ 1, Q: I have noticed that the Expression plots in Quickomics do not show the sample groups in the desired order after reordering the groups under “Groups and Samples”. This is not dataset dependent, I have found this feature not working across multiple datasets. Could you please provide a solution to this? A: This may due to the cache stored in your web browser. Please try to clean up the cache and restart Quickomics.
